items.title: Frank Wess interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Majesty of the Seas, May 29, 1995
items.q: he put me there because he knew I could play first if Marshall wasn’t there

ctx.x: Yeah, I told him to call Eric because you know I was playing third alto, and he put me there because he knew I could play first if Marshall wasn’t there, you know, he always kept somebody in the third chair that could play lead, so that he would never be without a lead player, you know. So he kept changing, looking for a tenor player, and it was bugging me, you know, because I’d played the book for what five or six years, you know what I mean? I knew what it was supposed to be. And he got all these people coming…
Who were some of your favorite drummers and bass players during that period?

items.title: 52222_Marshall Royal oral history interview
items.q: Frank West was an excellent arranger, although he did very little in the band.

ctx.x: In the early years in the Basie Band, we had probably the best jazz arrangers in the business. Ernie Wilkins in a premier arranger of jazz. Then we got a young dude out of the service by the name of Frank Foster and he was

a young genius. He could arrange anything of any mood, if you would just tie him down long enough. Frank West was an excellent arranger, although he did very little in the band. He was an excellent arranger. Then Thad Jones came into the band and he was a monster. He was latter-day Duke Ellington type arranger. That is the way that I feel.

When you mix other fellas like Billy Bauer, who is a genius in his own right in any phase of musical arrangement, along with the very healthy marriage that somehow or another came about with the Neal Hefti-Basie marriage there. They were good for each other. Neal Hefti couldn't sell none of his tunes with his own band, so he wrote them and gave them to Basie and we changed the tempos of all of them and played it our way and made him -- made his _______ rating go very high, which I'm sure he's thankful of, maybe.
